## What you'll be able to do {#outcomes}

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Keep your title/abstract screening decisions in a single, version-controlled file.
- Make a **commit** — a saved, labelled snapshot — and then **revise** a decision and
  commit again, leaving a clear history of who changed what, and when.
- Push your work so it is backed up and shareable.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Time:** ~30–45 min · **You'll produce:** a versioned `screening-log.csv` with at least
two commits, pushed to your own repository.
:::

## Why this matters {#why}

You already screen studies. The problem is rarely the screening — it is the *file*.
`screening_v3.xlsx`, then `screening_v3_FINAL.xlsx`, then `screening_v3_FINAL_really.xlsx`,
emailed back and forth until nobody can say which decision was made when, or by whom.

Version control fixes exactly this. You keep **one** file, and every time you change it
you save a labelled snapshot. The history *is* the audit trail a journal, funder, or
co-author would ask for — and you can always go back. Same screening work; reproducible.

## What you need {#prerequisites}

- VS Code, git, and a GitHub account (from the earlier setup steps).
- Your own copy of the exercise repository — you'll get this from the **Screening-log**
  assignment in Google Classroom (click the link, and GitHub makes you your own repo).

## Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

We'll use VS Code's built-in **Source Control** panel — buttons, not the terminal.

1. **Open your exercise repository in VS Code.** `File ▸ Open Folder…` and choose the
   folder you cloned from the assignment. You should see the project files on the left.
2. **Create the screening log.** Make a new file at the top level called
   `screening-log.csv` and give it these column headings on the first line:

   ```text
   study_id,title,decision,reason,screened_by,date
   ```

3. **Add at least three studies**, one per line. Each `decision` is `include` or
   `exclude`, with a short `reason`. For example:

   ```text
   S001,Cash transfers and school enrolment,include,RCT meeting our PICO,LS,2026-06-09
   S002,Opinion piece on education funding,exclude,Not an impact evaluation,LS,2026-06-09
   S003,Transfers and child labour: a quasi-experiment,include,Eligible design,LS,2026-06-09
   ```

4. **Make your first commit.** Open the **Source Control** panel (the branch icon on the
   left, or `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + G`). You'll see `screening-log.csv` listed under *Changes*.
   Type a message like `Add initial screening decisions` in the box and click
   **✓ Commit**. (If prompted to stage, click **Yes** / the **+** next to the file first.)

   > You have just saved a labelled snapshot. That is a commit.

5. **Revise a decision.** Re-reading an abstract, you change your mind: edit one row from
   `exclude` to `include` (or vice versa) and update its `reason`. Save the file.
6. **Commit again** with a message that says what changed, e.g.
   `Revise decision for S002 after re-reading`.
7. **Push your work.** Click **Sync Changes** (or the `…` menu ▸ *Push*) to send your
   commits to GitHub. Sign in if asked.

### Working with the agent {#agent}

You can ask Claude Code (in the VS Code terminal) or Copilot to help — for example,
*"add three more screening rows to screening-log.csv in the same format."* That is fine,
**but always read what it produced and check it** before you commit: open the file and
confirm the columns and decisions are right. The rule for the whole course: the agent
drafts, *you* verify. Never commit something you haven't read.

## Try it yourself {#try}

Complete the **Screening-log** assignment in Google Classroom.

> **Your task:** create `screening-log.csv` with the six columns and at least three
> `include`/`exclude` decisions, commit it, then revise one decision and commit again,
> and push.
>
> **Done when:** the file has the required columns and ≥3 rows, and there are **at least
> two commits** to it.

## Verify {#verify}

Don't just trust that it worked — confirm the history exists. In the VS Code terminal,
run:

```bash
git log --oneline -- screening-log.csv
```

You should see **at least two** commits (your initial decisions, then your revision).
That history is the proof of *how* your screening evolved. In Classroom, the assignment's
automatic check also turns green when your file and history are in order.

## Common pitfalls {#pitfalls}

- **Wrong file name or place.** It must be `screening-log.csv` at the top level of the
  repository — not inside a sub-folder, not `.xlsx`.
- **Capitalised decisions.** Use lower case: `include` / `exclude`.
- **One big commit.** The point is a *revision*, so commit your initial decisions first,
  then commit the change separately — that's what creates the history.
- **Forgetting to push.** Commits live on your computer until you **Sync/Push** them.

## Recap {#recap}

You put a real synthesis artefact — your screening decisions — under version control,
made two commits, and pushed them. You now have a tracked, recoverable history instead of
a pile of emailed spreadsheets. That same habit carries through every later stage of the
review.

Tier 1, where version control and reproducible documents become second nature.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Facilitator notes

- Expect the **commit vs push** distinction to be the main sticking point — show the
  Source Control panel live and point out that committed work is still only local until
  pushed.
- Watch for `.xlsx` habits: some will try to make a spreadsheet. Reinforce that plain
  CSV is what makes the history readable.
- Good moment to pair learners for a quick peer check of each other's commit history.
:::
